# Homework 3 - Tidyverse

## Conceptual Questions

1.  If your working directory is myfolder/homework/, what relative path would you specify to get the file located at myfolder/MyData.csv? 
    1. "../MyData.csv"
2.  What are the major benefits of using R projects?
    1.  I can create a project organization directly in RStudio, set the working directory, and manage git and github directly in RStudio (I love this!).
3.  What is Git and what is GitHub?
    1. Git is a version control software that is run locally on my computer.  It tracks changes to files and allows me to make those changes permanent or revert back to a previous version.
    2. GitHub is a cloud-based platform that hosts git repositories.  It is a remote backup of repositories.  It allows collaboration between team members by tracking changes and allowing each team member to upload their changes and others to pull those changes to their local environment.  It also tracks versions and will alert the team member if there are merge conflicts allowing the team member to decide how to handle the conflicts.
4.  What are the two main differences between a tibble and a data.frame?
    1. If one column is called from a tibble the tibble allows the column to remain a tibble instead of a vector.
    2. The tibble displays the data in a nicer format by only printing the data that is visible in the output.  It also lists the number of columns and rows along with all the column names and types.
    3. Tibbles do not automatically convert character variables to factors. 
    
## Reading Delimited Data

### Glass Data

Locate the glass data and read the comma separated values files into a tibble using the tidyverse function read_csv, but first load the library to load the functions in this session.

```{r}
library(readr)
#?read_csv
glass_data <- read_csv("https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/online/datasets/glass.data", col_names=c("Id", "RI", "Na", "Mg", "Al", "Si", "K", "Ca", "Ba", "Fe", "Type"))
glass_data
```

#### Combine Excel Files

##### White Wine

Read in the column names from the second sheet in the same white wine Excel file.

```{r}
wine_names <- read_excel(here("HW_3", "white-wine.xlsx"), sheet=2)
wine_names
```
Add the column names to the white wine data file
```{r}
colnames(white_wine_data) <- wine_names$Variables
white_wine_data
```

Add a new column that indicates all of the observations in the tibble are white wines.
```{r}
library(dplyr)
white_wine_data <- white_wine_data |> 
  mutate(type = 'White')
white_wine_data
```

##### Red Wine

Read in the semicolon delimited data into a red wine file.
```{r}
red_wine <- read_delim("https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/red-wine.csv", delim=';')
red_wine
```

Rename the columns for the red wine to match the columns from the white wine.

```{r}
colnames(red_wine) <- wine_names$Variables
red_wine
```

Add a new 'type' column and label each observation in the tibble as red.
```{r}
red_wine <- red_wine |> 
  mutate(type = 'red')
red_wine
```

Combine the white wine and red wine files to one file.
```{r}
?bind_rows
wine_data <- bind_rows(white_wine_data, red_wine)
wine_data
```

## Writing a Function

Write a function to calculate the IQR for a vector.  Remove any names and use unnamed arguments.
```{r}
?quantile
getIQR <- function(vector) {
  return(quantile(vector, 0.75, FALSE, FALSE)-quantile(vector,0.25, FALSE, FALSE))
}
```
Apply getIQR function to the wine data frame on the fixed acidity and citric acid columns
```{r}
getIQR(wine_data$fixed_acidity)
getIQR(wine_data$citric_acid)
```

Write a function to calculate the sample coefficient of variation by dividing the sample standard deviation by the absolute value of the mean.
```{r}
?sd
?abs
getCoefVar <- function(vector) {
  sd(vector)/abs(mean(vector))
}
```
Apply the getCoefVar function to the wine data frame on the fixed acidity and citric acid columns
```{r}
getCoefVar(wine_data$fixed_acidity)
getCoefVar(wine_data$citric_acid)
```

Create a function that returns both the IQR and Coefficient of variation for a given vector by calling the already created functions and naming each element.
```{r}
getSummaries <- function(vector) {
  return(c(IQR=getIQR(vector),Coef_Variation=getCoefVar(vector)))
}
```
Apply get summaries function to the wine data frame on the fixed acidity and citric acid columns.
```{r}
getSummaries(wine_data$fixed_acidity)
getSummaries(wine_data$citric_acid)
```

Write the infix function that can be used to add a data frame to a data frame or a vector.
```{r}
`%mybind%` <- function(df1, df2) {
  cbind(df1, df2)
}

```
Define the data frames and vector.  Change the vector to a data frame so there is a column label when combining the elements.
```{r}
df1 <- data.frame(unif = runif(10), norm = rnorm(10))
df2 <- data.frame(gamma = rgamma(10, shape = 1), beta = rbeta(10, shape1 = 5, shape2 = 1))
vec1 <- rnorm(10, mean = 10)
df1
df2
vec1
vec1_df <- data.frame(vec1)

```
Use the newly created infix function mybind to combine the data frames and vector defined above.  Combine both the vector and vector data frame separately.  Name the vector after combined or change to a data frame so it has a name.
```{r}
df1 %mybind% df2
df2 %mybind% vec1_df
df1 %mybind% df2 %mybind% vec1_df
combined <- df1 %mybind% df2 %mybind% vec1
names(combined) <- c('unif', 'norm', 'gamma', 'beta', 'vec1_norm')
combined
```
